> 「须陀洹名为入流，而无所入，不入色声香味触法，是名须陀洹。」……「阿那含名为不来，而实无不来，是故名阿那含。」

The ninth section walks through the four stages of the hearer's path, and defines each one by denying the word used to name it.

入流 but nothing entered. 一来 but no coming and going. 不来 but no non-coming. And finally the arhat, of whom it is said there is no dharma called arhat.

## The pattern is the point

Each definition has the same shape: the name, then the cancellation, then the name again as a conventional label. 名为入流，而无所入，是名须陀洹.

A stage of attainment is a description of what has stopped, not a rank that has been conferred. The vocabulary is a report, not a title.

## 入流 is about what you no longer flow into

须陀洹 — *stream-enterer* — is said to have entered the stream of the noble path, having cut the three fetters: belief in a self, attachment to rites, and doubt.

The sutra's gloss is sharper: 不入色声香味触法. The stream-enterer does not enter the six fields. Not does not perceive them — does not get carried into them.

The book is careful here, because the misreading is attractive: this is not closing the eyes and ears. The senses work. Seeing, hearing, tasting happen. What has stopped is the follow-through — the automatic move from perception to pursuit, from hearing a sound to wanting the source of it.

## 无诤三昧 and 阿兰那

须菩提 then reports his own attainment, and the phrase he uses is 无诤三昧 — the concentration of no contention — and 阿兰那, the quiet dwelling.

无诤 is not agreement. It is the absence of opposition in the mind: no comparing, no contesting, no positioning against another. Two people can disagree sharply without 诤, if neither is trying to win. And two people can agree entirely while 诤 runs underneath, each checking that the other still concurs.

This is why the section puts it here, among the fruits: the attainment being described is not a state of peace you enter, but a mode of relation you stop disturbing.

## 实无有法名阿罗汉

The last stage gets the strongest denial: there is no dharma called arhat.

An arhat has ended the afflictions and the round of birth-and-death. What the sutra denies is not that this happened; it denies that "arhat" names a thing someone has become.

The book's line about 习气 is worth keeping: even the arhat retains habits of speech and manner. What is gone is the affliction, not the personality. And what is definitively absent is the thought *I am an arhat* — because that thought would be the first fetter returning, in its most refined form.

## The test

Name a title you are wearing. Any title: professional, familial, moral, or spiritual. Something you would not mind being called.

Then ask the question this section asks: if the title were removed — if no one knew, and the behaviour continued — what would remain?

That residue is what 须陀洹 is pointing at. The behaviour continues. The name is just a name, used when useful.
